blocks.x: STAT 153 · Statistical Methods · Topic 3

Once data have been collected, the first job of a statistician (or a clinician) is to summarise them into a few meaningful numbers. This topic builds the three pillars of descriptive statistics — where the data are centred, how spread out they are, and where any individual value sits relative to the rest — and applies each one to real medical measurements.

3measures of central tendency you must know: mean, median and mode 5numbers in a five-number summary — min, Q1, Q2 (median), Q3, max — that build a boxplot 100percentiles divide an ordered data set into 100 equal parts; quartiles and deciles are special cases
By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Compute and interpret the mean, median and mode of a clinical data set, and explain why each is used differently in health sciences (average patient age, typical blood pressure, common disease occurrence).
2Compute and interpret the range, variance and standard deviation of a data set, and explain why dispersion matters for assessing patient variability and flagging abnormal values.
3Locate quartiles, deciles and percentiles in an ordered data set using their position formulas, for both odd- and even-sized samples.

4Construct and read a boxplot from a five-number summary, and use the position of the median and the length of the whiskers to judge whether a distribution is symmetric, positively skewed or negatively skewed.
5Explain the relationship between quartiles and percentiles (Q1 = P25, Q2 = P50 = median, Q3 = P75) and apply the general percentile position formula k(n + 1)/100.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Descriptive statistics Numerical and graphical methods used to summarise the essential features of a data set — where it is centred, how spread out it is, and how individual values are positioned relative to the rest — without drawing conclusions beyond the data itself.
Central tendency Describes the typical or central value of a data set (mean, median, mode) — a single number that represents "where the data cluster."

Dispersion (variation) Describes how spread out the data values are around the centre (range, variance, standard deviation) — two data sets can share the same mean yet differ enormously in how consistent the values are.

Quantiles (position measures) Values that divide an ordered data set into equal-sized groups — quartiles (4 parts), deciles (10 parts) and percentiles (100 parts) — telling you where a particular observation ranks within the whole distribution.
Central Tendency→ Dispersion→ Quartiles / Deciles / Percentiles→ Boxplots
Where the data cluster

Central tendency answers a simple clinical question: "what is the typical value?" — the typical age of a patient cohort, the typical blood pressure, the most common disease diagnosis. Mean, median and mode each answer this question in a slightly different way.
Measures of central tendency Describe the typical or central value of a data set. The three common measures are the mean, median and mode.
Mean, median and mode
Mean (x̄) The arithmetic average of all observations. x̄ = Σx / n — sum all the observed values (Σx) and divide by the number of observations (n).

Median The middle value when the data are arranged in order (ascending or descending). For an odd number of observations it is the single middle value; for an even number it is the average of the two middle values. The median is not distorted by extreme outliers the way the mean can be.
Mode The most frequently occurring value in the data set. A data set can have one mode, more than one mode, or no mode at all if every value occurs equally often.
Use in health sciences

items: 1Average patient age — the mean age of patients admitted with a condition helps target screening and resource planning.
2Typical blood pressure level — a mean or median systolic/diastolic reading summarises a group's cardiovascular status at a glance.
3Common disease occurrence — the mode identifies the most frequently diagnosed condition in a clinic or ward, guiding where attention is most needed.

blocks.x: Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)
Systolic blood pressure readings were taken from 7 patients: 118, 120, 122, 125, 130, 130, 140 mmHg. Find the mean, median and mode.

items: 1Compute the mean: sum all 7 readings and divide by n = 7.x̄ = (118 + 120 + 122 + 125 + 130 + 130 + 140) / 7 = 885 / 7
2Simplify.x̄ ≈ 126.4 mmHg
3Find the median: the data are already ordered, and with n = 7 (odd) the median is the 4th value.118, 120, 122, 125, 130, 130, 140 → Median = 125 mmHg
4Find the mode: identify the value that occurs most often.130 mmHg appears twice — every other value appears once → Mode = 130 mmHg

blocks.x: Answer: Mean = 126.4 mmHg, Median = 125 mmHg, Mode = 130 mmHg. Interpretation: the typical systolic blood pressure in this group is about 126 mmHg.

blocks.title: Why report all three, not just the mean?

items: The mean uses every value but is pulled by extreme readings (e.g. one very high hypertensive reading can inflate it).
The median is resistant to outliers, so it is often preferred for skewed clinical data such as hospital stay lengths or income.
The mode is the only measure that makes sense for categorical clinical data, such as the most commonly diagnosed condition on a ward.

blocks.x: How spread out are the data?

Two groups of patients can have exactly the same mean blood glucose yet very different clinical risk, depending on how consistent (or scattered) their individual readings are. Dispersion measures capture that spread.
Measures of dispersion (variation) Show how spread out data values are around the centre. The common measures are the range, variance and standard deviation.
Range, variance and standard deviation
Range The difference between the maximum and minimum values in the data set. Range = x_max − x_min
Variance (s²) The average of the squared deviations of each observation from the mean, divided by n − 1 (for a sample). s² = Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1)
Standard deviation (s) The square root of the variance, bringing the measure of spread back into the same units as the original data (e.g. mmol/L rather than mmol²/L²). s = √s²
Why dispersion matters in medicine

items: 1Assess patient variability — a small standard deviation means patients are responding similarly (e.g. to a treatment); a large one means responses vary widely and may need individualised care.
2Identify abnormal values — dispersion measures set the scale for deciding how far a single reading must be from the mean before it is flagged as unusual or clinically concerning.

blocks.x: Fasting blood glucose levels (mmol/L)
Fasting blood glucose levels of 6 patients: 4.8, 5.1, 5.3, 6.0, 7.2, 9.0 mmol/L. Find the range and the (approximate) standard deviation.

items: 1Compute the range: maximum minus minimum.Range = 9.0 − 4.8 = 4.2 mmol/L
2Compute the mean, needed for variance.x̄ = (4.8 + 5.1 + 5.3 + 6.0 + 7.2 + 9.0) / 6 = 37.4 / 6 ≈ 6.23 mmol/L
3Square each deviation from the mean and sum them.Σ(x − x̄)² ≈ 2.05 + 1.28 + 0.87 + 0.05 + 0.93 + 7.65 ≈ 12.85
4Divide by n − 1 = 5 to get the variance, then take the square root.s² = 12.85 / 5 ≈ 2.57 → s = √2.57 ≈ 1.6 mmol/L

blocks.x: Answer: Range = 4.2 mmol/L, Standard deviation s ≈ 1.6 mmol/L. Interpretation: the large spread indicates variation in glycemic control across these patients — some may be at risk of diabetes.

blocks.title: Range vs. standard deviation — when does each fall short?

items: The range uses only the two extreme values, so a single unusually high or low reading dominates it while ignoring everything in between.
The standard deviation uses every observation, giving a more complete picture of spread, which is why it is preferred for clinical variability assessments.
Both range and standard deviation are always non-negative — a value of zero means every observation in the data set is identical.

sections.title: Dividing data into four equal parts

blocks.x: Where does a value rank?

Beyond "typical value" and "spread," clinicians often need to know where one particular reading ranks within a whole population — is this patient's cholesterol in the top 10%? Quartiles, deciles and percentiles answer exactly that, and boxplots turn the answer into a picture.
Dividing data into four equal parts

Quartiles Values that divide an ordered data set into four equal parts. For ungrouped data with n observations: Position of Q1 = (n + 1) / 4 Position of Q2 = 2(n + 1) / 4 = (n + 1) / 2 (the Median) Position of Q3 = 3(n + 1) / 4 Q4 is simply the maximum value in the data set.
Given the ordered data 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 (n = 7), find Q1, Q2, Q3 and Q4.

items: 1Find the position of Q1.Position of Q1 = (7 + 1) / 4 = 8 / 4 = 2 → the 2nd value → Q1 = 6
2Find the position of Q2 (the median).Position of Q2 = 8 / 2 = 4 → the 4th value → Q2 = 10
3Find the position of Q3.Position of Q3 = 3(8) / 4 = 24 / 4 = 6 → the 6th value → Q3 = 14
4Q4 is simply the maximum value.Q4 = 16

blocks.x: The boxplot

Boxplot (box-and-whisker plot) A graphical display built from the five-number summary: minimum, Q1, Q2 (median), Q3, and maximum. A box is drawn from Q1 to Q3 (marking the median inside it), with "whiskers" extending out to the minimum and maximum.
Reading the median's position

If the median line sits near the centre of the box, the distribution is approximately symmetric. If it falls toward the left of the box, the distribution is positively skewed. If it falls toward the right of the box, the distribution is negatively skewed.
Reading the whisker lengths

If the two whiskers are about the same length, the distribution is approximately symmetric. If the right whisker is longer, the distribution is positively skewed. If the left whisker is longer, the distribution is negatively skewed.
The number of meteorites found in 10 US states: 89, 47, 164, 296, 30, 215, 138, 78, 48, 39. Construct the five-number summary for a boxplot.

items: 1Order the data from smallest to largest.30, 39, 47, 48, 78, 89, 138, 164, 215, 296
2Read off the minimum and maximum.Min = 30, Max = 296
3With n = 10 (even), Q2 is the average of the two middle values (5th and 6th).Q2 = (78 + 89) / 2 = 83.5
4Q1 is the median of the lower half and Q3 is the median of the upper half of the ordered data.Q1 = 47, Q3 = 164

blocks.x: Five-number summary: Min = 30, Q1 = 47, Q2 = 83.5, Q3 = 164, Max = 296.
Dividing data into ten equal parts
Deciles Divide an ordered data set into 10 equal parts. The k-th decile (Dk) is the value below which k × 10% of the data lie, where k = 1, 2, …, 9. Position of Dk = k(n + 1) / 10
Given the ordered data 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19 (n = 9), find the 4th decile (D4).

items: 1Substitute k = 4 and n = 9 into the position formula.Position of D4 = 4(9 + 1) / 10 = 40 / 10 = 4
2Read off the 4th value in the ordered data.3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19

blocks.x: Answer: D4 = 9.
Dividing data into a hundred equal parts
Percentiles Divide an ordered data set into 100 equal parts. The k-th percentile (Pk) is the value below which k% of the data lie, where k = 1, 2, …, 99. Position of Pk = k(n + 1) / 100
Given the ordered data 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26 (n = 9), find the 75th percentile (P75).

items: 1Substitute k = 75 and n = 9 into the position formula.Position of P75 = 75(9 + 1) / 100 = 750 / 100 = 7.5
2A position of 7.5 falls halfway between the 7th and 8th values, so average them.7th value = 22, 8th value = 24
3Average the 7th and 8th values.P75 = (22 + 24) / 2 = 23

blocks.x: Answer: P75 = 23.
Relationship between quartiles and percentiles

Quartiles are special-case percentiles
Both use the same general position formula, Position of P<sub>k</sub> = k(n + 1) / 100, and quartiles are simply the percentiles at k = 25, 50 and 75.

blocks.title: Quick self-check: quartiles, deciles and percentiles

items: All three (quartiles, deciles, percentiles) require the data to be ordered first — the position formulas are meaningless on unsorted data.
When a computed position is a whole number, read off that exact ranked value. When it falls between two ranks (like 7.5), average the two surrounding values.

A patient's reading at the 90th percentile for a measurement is higher than about 90% of the reference population's readings — useful for growth charts, cholesterol screening and lab reference ranges.
